title: Chinese Study Warns Beijing Against Defense Contractor Influence, Citing US 'Iron Triangle'; Brookings Experts Doubt Golden Dome Can End the Arms Race
subhead: A Shanghai Jiao Tong University study published Monday cautions Beijing that profit-driven defense contractors can hijack national security policy, pointing to the US military-industrial complex as a cautionary example — while Brookings analysts argue Trump's Golden Dome missile shield may accelerate, not end, the nuclear arms race with China and Russia.

sections.heading: Chinese Study Warns Beijing About Defense Contractor Influence
sections.body:
A new study from China's Shanghai Jiao Tong University National Institute of Strategic Studies warns Beijing of the danger of defense contractors gaining too much influence over defense policy, pointing to the profit-driven expansion of the US military-industrial complex as a cautionary example, SCMP reports. Researchers said Washington's 'iron triangle' — linking the Department of Defence, private contractors and congressional committees — had hijacked US national security policy.

Lead author Gu Jianyi, a former researcher at a military institute, wrote that contractors, the military and politicians form a mutually reinforcing alliance where profits, expanded budgets and political capital align, creating a 'self-perpetuating cycle of military expansion, increased revenue, mutual benefit, further expansion' that drives armament growth independent of external security pressures. 'The core flaw of the US military-industrial complex is that capital profit-seeking overrides national security and public interest,' he wrote, warning that lobbying, manufactured conflicts and threat perception create an inherent risk of 'expanding armaments merely for profit.'
sections.whyItMatters: The study signals how Beijing is framing its own defense-industrial policy in explicit contrast to the US model — a warning against letting commercial interests drive procurement. It also reflects a deliberate Chinese narrative that US rearmament is profit-driven rather than threat-driven, useful ammunition in the arms-control debate as Washington pours record sums into replenishment.

sections.heading: Brookings Experts Doubt Golden Dome Can End the Nuclear Arms Race
sections.body:
US President Donald Trump's plan to build a national missile defense system, dubbed the Golden Dome, may not fully protect America and could accelerate the global arms race involving China, Russia and North Korea, according to experts speaking at a Brookings Institution discussion, SCMP reports. University of Maryland professor Steve Fetter said the current expansion of China's nuclear arsenal, including the estimated construction of 350 new missile silos, has been motivated 'at least in part' by US missile defenses.

'It's not clear that, at the end of the day, we will be any less vulnerable to a nuclear attack after these actions and reactions,' Fetter said. Brookings research director Michael O'Hanlon emphasized that deploying missile defense tends to 'run the risk of creating an arms race,' because whoever is having the defense deployed against them tends to overestimate, while whoever is building the defense tends to compensate in the other way.
sections.whyItMatters: The critique lands as the Pentagon and its contractors — including Arcfield, which is positioning itself as a Golden Dome mission-engineering partner — begin scaling up for the program. If the analysis holds, the multi-billion-dollar shield could trigger exactly the Chinese and Russian force expansion it is meant to counter, undercutting the strategic rationale for the investment.

sections.heading: Trump Tech Strategy Favors Drone Swarms and Big Tech AI
sections.body:
The White House's new national security technology strategy (NSSTS) pushes faster development of emerging military technologies, gives defense innovators more room to experiment, and broadens the federal market for young defense tech startups, Defense One reports. The strategy sets specific 'priority areas' for new military research and spending — undersea, space, and AI and autonomy — and calls for 'optimal combinations of lower-cost (and sometimes lower-tech or attritable) platforms that can be deployed in larger numbers,' including drone swarms alongside manned assets.

It pushes Pentagon buyers to bypass traditional acquisitions in favor of performance-based contracts and other transaction authorities (OTAs), and takes aim at foreign military sales rules and export controls that hobble the sale of defense tech to allies. But the strategy also comes down on the side of Big Tech companies pushing an energy-intensive AI future over open-weight approaches, which analysts say could benefit China and slow the US military from getting the tools commanders want.
sections.whyItMatters: The strategy is a concrete policy turn toward attritable, mass-produced systems over a smaller number of exquisite platforms — the same logic driving the Replicator program, which has received only about $1 billion in its first two years. Its AI stance, however, risks concentrating capability in a few well-connected firms at a moment when the Pentagon is trying to broaden its supplier base.

sections.heading: DISA Awards Peraton $953M Communications Infrastructure Contract
sections.body:
The Defense Information Systems Agency (DISA) has awarded Peraton a potential 10-year, $953 million contract to continue providing communication infrastructure services for data centers and hybrid cloud computing environments, Defense One reports. The award covers the third iteration of DISA's Capacity Services Communications (CSC III) contract, which received three proposals.

CSC III emphasizes on-demand communications capabilities, letting the agency adjust requirements based on mission needs rather than a fixed equipment set. Peraton is tasked with providing hardware, operating software, storage, network management tools and automation software across DISA and non-DISA sites worldwide, over an initial five-year base period plus up to five option years. Peraton inherited the CSC program in 2021 through its combination with Perspecta, which had purchased longtime incumbent Knight Point Systems in 2019.
sections.whyItMatters: The recompete win locks Peraton into a core piece of the Pentagon's communications backbone for a decade, and the shift to on-demand capacity reflects a broader move away from fixed infrastructure toward flexible, mission-driven IT — a pattern the Pentagon is applying across its enterprise services.

sections.heading: Arcfield Eyes Etalon Manufacturing as Golden Dome Work Ramps Up
sections.body:
Defense and aerospace company Arcfield is preparing for an upcoming satellite launch and exploring manufacturing of etalons — highly polished glass components key for optical sensors and laser communications — as it positions itself in the Golden Dome missile-defense program, Defense One reports from the Space and Missile Defense Symposium in Huntsville, Alabama.

Arcfield's subsidiary Orion Space Solutions expects to launch a very low Earth orbit (VLEO) satellite in September, and the company is forging geostationary orbit satellite plans for 2027 while supporting Golden Dome with mission engineering. Vice president Dan Knight said the company wants to expand etalon production to reduce reliance on foreign suppliers, seeking government funding through the Pentagon's Manufacturing Technology (ManTech) program. Separately, Germany's Luftwaffe officially changed its English name to the German Air and Space Force, with Maj. Gen. Michael Traut saying the air and space domains are 'increasingly merging' and that Germany wants to procure space surveillance radars.
sections.whyItMatters: Arcfield's push to onshore etalon manufacturing illustrates how Golden Dome is pulling specialized optical-component production back to the US industrial base — a microcosm of the broader effort to reduce dependence on foreign suppliers for national security technology, even as Germany moves to mirror the US in merging air and space command.

sections.heading: Taiwan Runs First Live-Fire Exercise With FPV Drones Against Armored Vehicles
sections.body:
Taiwan's army has for the first time used first-person view (FPV) drones against armored vehicles in a live-fire exercise, adopting tactics pioneered during the Ukraine war to strengthen its asymmetric capabilities against the People's Liberation Army, SCMP reports. The exercise on Monday brought together six units from the army's artillery commands, Marine Corps and Military Police under the Army Unmanned Systems Training Command.

Under simulated battlefield conditions, operators flew FPV drones carrying armor-piercing warheads against decommissioned tanks and armored ammunition carriers, conducting frontal and flanking strikes in both single-drone and coordinated two-drone attacks, according to the defense ministry-affiliated Youth Daily News. The exercise highlights efforts to broaden strike options beyond traditional firepower such as rocket systems and heavy artillery.
sections.whyItMatters: The drill marks Taiwan's formal adoption of the FPV-drone tactics that have reshaped the Ukraine battlefield, signaling a shift toward cheap, attritable strike systems in its asymmetric defense posture. It comes as Taiwan also pursues indigenous drone and space capabilities, though a locally developed satellite launcher failed its first test this week, triggering a brief missile panic.

sections.heading: Trump's Offensive Cyber Program Faces Russia Hurdle
sections.body:
President Trump's plan to enlist private companies to help disrupt cybercriminals abroad may face a fundamental problem in Russia: distinguishing criminal hackers from state-backed operatives, Defense One reports. Russian intelligence services have long tolerated, protected or intermittently recruited financially motivated hackers without exercising full control over them, giving Moscow easier access to hacking talent.

The program's targeting criteria require that a group not be part of, or wholly controlled by, a foreign government unless 'clear intelligence' establishes that connection. But analysts say Russia's cyber landscape is opaque and shifting, blurring lines between government and cybercriminal. 'Russia's cyber web is opaque and always shifting, blurring lines between government and cybercriminal, with no single rule for understanding each and every relationship,' said Justin Sherman, CEO of Global Cyber Strategies.
sections.whyItMatters: The program — part of the White House's push to authorize private-sector offensive cyber action — runs into the same attribution problem that has long complicated US policy toward Russian cybercrime. The ambiguity is partly intentional, allowing the Kremlin to expand the pool of hackers it can covertly draw upon, which limits how much private companies can safely target.

bottomLine: Today's defense news is dominated by the strategic debate over how the US is rearming and what it signals to rivals. A Chinese study explicitly warns Beijing against letting defense contractors drive policy, citing the US 'iron triangle' as a cautionary example, while Brookings analysts argue Trump's Golden Dome missile shield may accelerate rather than end the nuclear arms race with China and Russia. On the industrial side, the White House's new tech strategy pushes drone swarms and attritable systems while favoring Big Tech AI, DISA locked Peraton into a $953 million communications contract, and Arcfield is onshoring specialized optical-component production for Golden Dome. In the Indo-Pacific, Taiwan formally adopted Ukraine-style FPV drone tactics in its first live-fire exercise against armored vehicles. The through-line is a US defense establishment scaling up on multiple fronts — missile defense, munitions, space, cyber — even as analysts and rivals question whether the buildup achieves its strategic aims or simply provokes a matching response.
sources: SCMP, Defense One, Brookings Institution, Shanghai Jiao Tong University National Institute of Strategic Studies, Youth Daily News
